transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-09-30
Time: 14:00 UTC
Duration: ~58 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Desai (Redwood SE), Marcus Chen (CTO - Crimson), Lina Gómez (ML Eng), Tom Alvarez (Infra)
---
[00:00:00] Jordan Lee: okay everyone i'm gonna kick off, um thanks for carving out the time. we're planning to focus on throughput tuning—specifically how continuous batching and the scheduler knobs interact with your peak bursts.
[00:00:20] Marcus Chen: yeah thanks jordan. we've been hitting some weird p95 spikes during our evening batch jobs, and we think it correlates to some long sequences and cold kv cache misses.
[00:00:35] Priya Desai: makes sense. can you give a quick baseline? what does your QPS mix look like and average seq len?
[00:00:45] Lina Gómez: so typical mix is 70% short chat responses (<= 128 tokens), 20% medium (128-512), 10% long generation up to 2k. avg seq length ~210 tokens. peak qps ~420, sustained ~230.
[00:01:10] Jordan Lee: great, that helps. two immediate knobs we usually look at: max_num_seqs (aka the simultaneous sequences per GPU scheduler allows) and the token guard / max_tokens_per_request which protects token budget for very long requests.
[00:01:28] Tom Alvarez: how aggressive can max_num_seqs be? last time we cranked to 128 and saw throughput but p95 went way up.
[00:01:36] Priya Desai: right, increasing max_num_seqs increases packing and throughput but it raises tail latency because batching blocks on the slowest sequence. essentially you trade single-request latency for system-level throughput. that said, there are scheduler knobs to soften that impact — priority classes and heartbeat/lease timeouts.
[00:01:55] Speaker 2: (auto) can you explain heartbeat?
[00:02:00] Priya Desai: heartbeat is how often a worker reports liveness to the scheduler and how long a batch waits for late arrivals before dispatch. there's a 'soft_wait' and a 'hard_wait' — soft waits allow partial flush if deadline hits; hard wait is absolute. tuning soft vs hard lets you avoid waiting for a single long seq at cost of slightly lower packing.
[00:02:24] Marcus Chen: okay, so we shouldn't just max out max_num_seqs. we also need to adjust waits. what's a sane starting point?
[00:02:31] Priya Desai: for your mix i'd suggest max_num_seqs=64 as a starting point, soft_wait=12-18ms, hard_wait=120ms, and token_guard multiplier of 1.2 to avoid token explosion from a long request.
[00:02:45] Lina Gómez: token_guard? we use max_tokens_per_request of 2048 currently. is that enough?
[00:02:52] Priya Desai: max_tokens_per_request=2048 is fine, token_guard is a workload scaler — you can multiply expected tokens by guard to back off when a seq is unexpectedly large. it prevents one long seq from starving others.
[00:03:05] Jordan Lee: quick callout — KV cache hit-rate interacts a lot here. if your KV cache is cold, those long gens are expensive and blow up latencies. so warming is critical for workload with many long sequence requests.
[00:03:20] Tom Alvarez: we saw kv-hitrate ~22% on long sessions after a deploy. how do we warm effectively?
[00:03:27] Priya Desai: typical approaches: prefetching common prefixes during off-peak windows, TTL tuning to keep hot entries longer, and using sticky routing for sessions that expect long continuations — sticky keeps the same worker and KV set so you avoid cross-node misses.
[00:03:45] Speaker 3: (auto) sticky routing sounds like stateful; does that affect packing?
[00:03:50] Priya Desai: good question. sticky routing reduces cross-worker KV misses but does reduce pooling opportunities across workers because requests are pinned — that can lower packing efficiency. it's a tradeoff: for very chatty sessions it usually pays off. for short requests, don't use sticky.
[00:04:07] Marcus Chen: what about quantization? we experimented with int8 and saw some small hallucinations, but massive cost wins.
[00:04:15] Priya Desai: quantization saves cycles but can change model logits distribution, which sometimes causes odd token selections especially on long sequences. one pattern we recommend: use quantized variant for short/medium requests and fallback to fp16 for critical long generations. Redwood runtime supports automatic model-variants routing so you can do that at policy level.
[00:04:36] Jordan Lee: we'll share an example policy JSON — routing by max_tokens_per_request or by endpoint.
[00:04:44] Lina Gómez: ok. any kernel-level knobs? we run on A100s in your dedicated cluster.
[00:04:50] Priya Desai: kernel selection is automatic but we expose 'continuous_batching' parameters: batch_size_threshold, max_latency_ms, and eval_interval for the scheduler. for A100s, letting the runtime pick tiled kernels for attention gives best perf. the knobs to play with: increase eval_interval slightly so the scheduler keeps steady batches instead of thrashing on tiny arrivals.
[00:05:10] Tom Alvarez: eval_interval meaning how often scheduler tries to form batches?
[00:05:13] Priya Desai: exactly. default is 8ms; bump to 12-16ms if you have a lot of short requests to improve packing without hurting p95 terribly.
[00:05:24] Jordan Lee: also consider request shaping at the client side — 429/backpressure is expensive; instead try smoothing spikes with a modest token bucket, that keeps the scheduler happier.
[00:05:35] Marcus Chen: that's on our roadmap — but we can't change all clients.
[00:05:39] Priya Desai: then server-side admission controls are key. soft priority classes let you throttle best-effort traffic in bursts. configure a lower priority queue for non-critical async calls.
[00:05:50] Speaker 2: (auto) can you show an example config?
[00:05:52] Jordan Lee: yes we'll send an example scheduler.yaml and a short readme.
[00:05:58] [00:06:10] (brief silence, file-sharing note)
[00:06:20] Jordan Lee: quick digression — you mentioned VPC/on-prem constraints earlier; any network egress limits or strict firewall rules?
[00:06:28] Tom Alvarez: Egress is rate-limited in our corp VPC and some tenant networks are air-gapped. for private deployments we need guidance on offline image sizes and KMS setup.
[00:06:40] Priya Desai: for on-prem we ship a trimmed runtime image and we have a dry-run for KMS integration. we'll attach our private-deploy notes. offline image size can be reduced with model quantization and stripped debug kernels.
[00:06:55] Marcus Chen: curious about latency SLOs. if we set p95 < 250ms for short requests, can Redwood guarantee that with these knobs?
[00:07:04] Priya Desai: under most mixes yes. short requests benefit from lower soft_wait and sticky disabled. the wild card is KV cache misses and external DB calls—those are outside the runtime. so we aim for p95 < 250ms if cache hit-rate > 80% and no heavy long-gen interference.
[00:07:25] Lina Gómez: ok that's helpful.
[00:07:28] Jordan Lee: let's step through a concrete experiment plan — Priya, you had suggested a 1-hour continuous-batch run, right?
[00:07:34] Priya Desai: yes. test matrix I'd run: (A) baseline current config, (B) max_num_seqs=64 + soft_wait=15ms + hard_wait=120ms, (C) same as B + token_guard=1.2 + sticky routing only for session-type long-gen, (D) conservative: max_num_seqs=32 + bump eval_interval to 16ms. capture p50/p95/p99, token throughput, kv hit-rate, GPU util, and queueing depth.
[00:08:05] Tom Alvarez: we'll be able to reproduce traffic mix locally and in a staging cluster — we'll run both.
[00:08:12] Marcus Chen: what data should we send you?
[00:08:15] Priya Desai: upload a 48h request trace (timestamps, token counts, endpoints, session id) and indicate which endpoints are critical. also include current autoscaler and GPU instance types.
[00:08:28] Jordan Lee: we'll provide a csv template.
[00:08:32] [00:08:45] Jordan Lee: some gotchas from other customers — watch out for token limits on proxies and API gateways which clip long requests and cause mid-seq truncation. that shows up very weirdly in metrics.
[00:08:59] Lina Gómez: we saw that once — a buggy NGINX plugin truncated bodies. nightmare.
[00:09:05] Priya Desai: another gotcha: if you enable cross-worker KV replication aggressively it can increase tail latency due to synchronization. prefer eventual replication and stickiness for hot sessions.
[00:09:18] Marcus Chen: you mentioned warmup strategies earlier — could you spell out a simple cron we could run to prefetch KV keys?
[00:09:25] Priya Desai: simple approach: nightly job that replays top N session prefixes from 24h windows into the KV store with TTL equal to your hottest window. We'll attach an example script.
[00:09:40] Speaker 2: (auto) can you quantify the cost of warmup?
[00:09:44] Priya Desai: the cost is extra tokens and compute off-peak; but usually small compared to p95 tail impact during peaks. you'll trade maybe 3-5% extra token usage for 30-50% reduction in p95 in worst-case scenarios.
[00:09:58] Jordan Lee: let's talk about a scenic point — throttling/priority and token caps during deploys. many teams run canaries; what to do if a canary saturates the batcher?
[00:10:09] Priya Desai: run the canary on a separate priority or tenant, limit its max_num_seqs or weight. also set circuit-breakers to failover to a smaller model if latency climbs.
[00:10:20] Marcus Chen: do you support automatic fallback to quantized variant?
[00:10:23] Priya Desai: yes it can be policy-driven. but be mindful of any quality checks — we recommend routing flagged requests to fp16 for scoring.
[00:10:33] [00:10:40] (file share: redwood/scheduler-examples/seq-governor.yaml)
[00:10:45] Jordan Lee: sending the link in chat now — it's a minimal example.
[00:10:50] Lina Gómez: thanks.
[00:11:00] [00:11:12] Jordan Lee: quick interruption — can we capture GPU kernel stats? we like to see per-kernel time to ensure the tiled attention is being used.
[00:11:20] Priya Desai: yep runtime exposes a kernel-profile endpoint and we can dump periodic traces. for A100s you'll see conv/attention tiled kernels dominate for larger seq lengths.
[00:11:33] Tom Alvarez: how heavy are the traces? do they blow up storage?
[00:11:36] Priya Desai: traces are lightweight if you sample 1%. full traces are heavier; we'd recommend sampling unless you need deep post-mortem.
[00:11:46] [00:12:00] Marcus Chen: let's get concrete — Priya, you said start with max_num_seqs=64. are there any cluster-level changes we should make to accomodate that?
[00:12:09] Priya Desai: ensure your pod-level resource limits allow for higher interleaving — more threads, slightly higher reserved GPU mem for kv cache. also check your node-level cgroup configs; bursting with too small CPU shares can cause kernel preemption and jitter.
[00:12:27] Jordan Lee: we saw a customer with p95 spikes traced to cpu steal on host due to cron jobs. ops folks should audit host background tasks.
[00:12:36] Lina Gómez: noted.
[00:12:40] [00:12:50] (15m mark summary) Jordan Lee: recap so far — suggested config changes (max_num_seqs=64, soft_wait~15ms, hard_wait~120ms, token_guard 1.2), warmup cron for KV, sticky for long sessions only, and quantization routing policy. action items: run bench, upload traces, share config.
[00:13:10] Marcus Chen: sounds good. let's tee up the benchmark details.
[00:13:15] Priya Desai: benchmark traffic should mimic peak mix with 1) ramp to steady state, 2) inject 5-10% long sequences at random, 3) run 1 hour. collect: p50/p95/p99, GPU util, queue depth, kv hit-rate, and model variant routing counts.
[00:13:36] Tom Alvarez: we'll run in staging and a smaller run on prod-lite.
[00:13:40] [00:13:50] (mid-call drift to quantization micro-discussion)
[00:14:00] Priya Desai: small note on quantization: per-layer outlier detection can be used — keep a small fp16 head for safety. implement validation hooks to compare token distributions on a sample set.
[00:14:15] Marcus Chen: is there an eval harness you recommend?
[00:14:20] Priya Desai: we'll share a lightweight eval harness that compares top-k distributions and perplexity on your sample prompts. it's in the repo link we'll send.
[00:14:30] Jordan Lee: ok moving towards scheduling details — heartbeat intervals, lease durations, and how they affect requeueing.
[00:14:38] Priya Desai: heartbeat shorter than your network jitter is bad; set heartbeat to ~2x median RTT. leases should be slightly above expected compute time for your long sequences. if lease expires, scheduler will reassign and that can duplicate work. so set conservative leases for long-gens.
[00:14:59] Tom Alvarez: what's the duplication detection like?
[00:15:02] Priya Desai: request ids and idempotency tokens help; the runtime will drop duplicates if the same id is seen twice within a window. implement idempotency on client side where possible.
[00:15:12] [00:15:30] (customer question on autoscaler interaction)
[00:15:33] Marcus Chen: how does autoscaler interact with higher max_num_seqs? could we end up with underprovisioning because scheduler uses more packing?
[00:15:42] Priya Desai: autoscaler should consider both GPU util and queue depth. if you pack more efficiently you might see lower GPU util but higher queueing — so tune autoscaler triggers to include sustained queue depth > threshold. Redwood Console exposes token-level cost and queue metrics to feed autoscaler decisions.
[00:16:00] Lina Gómez: is there sample alerting thresholds?
[00:16:03] Priya Desai: common pattern: scale up when queue depth > 1000 tokens for > 30s at 95th percentile; scale down when queue depth < 200 tokens for > 2m and GPU util < 60%. we'll include these as recommendations.
[00:16:18] Jordan Lee: I'm going to paste the recommended thresholds in the chat.
[00:16:25] [00:16:40] (longspan of discussion about traces, skipped here)
[00:20:10] Priya Desai: one more interesting knob: 'max_seqs_per_priority' — you can cap how many sequences a single priority class can occupy to protect critical traffic.
[00:20:20] Marcus Chen: ah that would let us keep the critical endpoints stable while letting async jobs bulk up.
[00:20:24] Priya Desai: exactly. and combined with token guards it's pretty robust.
[00:20:30] [00:21:00] (noise about historical incidents and mitigation strategies)
[00:24:00] Jordan Lee: nearing the tail of the session — any last deep technical Qs?
[00:24:05] Lina Gómez: how to instrument kv cache hit rate in the runtime?
[00:24:09] Priya Desai: runtime exposes kv.hitrate and kv.misses counters and per-session metrics; we recommend aggregating by endpoint and session length. to correlate, join with token counts in your metrics pipeline.
[00:24:25] Marcus Chen: and alerts on sudden drop of hit-rate?
[00:24:29] Priya Desai: yes: alert if hit-rate drops below 60% for > 5m during peak windows.
[00:24:36] [00:25:00] (wrap-up and recap)
[00:25:05] Jordan Lee: final recap — we'll do the bench, share configs, and follow up. anything else?
[00:25:12] Tom Alvarez: please include the example warmup cron and the sticky routing sample.
[00:25:18] Priya Desai: will include both.
[00:25:22] Marcus Chen: thanks everyone, very helpful.
[00:25:25] Jordan Lee: thanks all. we'll sync on results next week.
[00:25:30] (call ends)

Notes on transcription: some speaker labels were auto-applied as Speaker 2/3; a few technical terms are slightly mangled (k v cache vs KV cache, max_n_seq vs max_num_seqs) — original audio file attached in CRM.
